articles.title: Google Discovers Unexpected Patterns In AI Image Generation via @sejournal, @martinibuster
articles.fullContent:
A new Google research paper shows how the company can identify what users are doing with Nano Banana without violating user privacy. They subsequently discovered five different ways image generation is used. The Problem And Solution

People are uploading sensitive images of themselves and their families to Nano Banana so the concern about privacy is real. Yet, AI image generation is wildly popular and understanding how people use Nano Banana is crucial to identifying how it’s applied and what can be done to improve it for the different and emerging ways it’s being used. So the challenge was to identify a way for understanding how Nano Banana was being used while also respecting user privacy. The research paper explains: “Beyond proactive self-reports in traditional media and on social networks, there is limited data on how and why many people are using LLM image generation. With this growth in usage and emergent use cases, we sought to provide some descriptive analysis of Nano Banana use, to help understand the ways in which users might find tools like Nano Banana helpful for social connections, educational materials, scientific advancement, commerce, and more.”

The researchers proposed that they can understand how people use AI image generation by analyzing patterns in their text prompts and conversations, without needing to examine the uploaded or generated images themselves, while protecting user privacy. The researchers used an existing system called Urania, an existing framework Google already uses for gaining insights from LLM chat interactions. Analysis & Findings

The researchers analyzed 2.1 million Gemini Nano Banana conversations and grouped them into five categories: Social & Viral

They also compared how people used the technology across those five categories, examining: Artistic styles

1. Image Editing Features This activity includes removing objects and people from an image, modifying a background, adding new elements, and modifying images by resizing or restoring them. “Image Editing included explicit requests for modifications to alter, clean up, or change specific elements within an image that has already been created (or a reference image uploaded by a user). “

Artistic styles is another interesting feature where researchers discovered that users were asking for specific art mediums like watercolors, pencil sketches, photography style, or images like oil paintings. Other users vibed their images by describing moods or styles like minimalist, film noir, or vintage. Some of the more creative users requested conceptual mashups that paired clashing styles or moods. The researchers explained: “Artistic Style included explicit user requests about the creative direction and visual aesthetic, from the artistic medium used to specific stylistic or cultural influences. …Absurdity or Humor: Requests that intentionally incorporate elements of nonsense, satire, surreal comedy, or humorous exaggeration. Imitate Art, Person, or Character: Explicit requests to emulate the distinct style of a specific artist, public figure, or fictional character.”

3. Image Composition Within the five category of uses they also noticed that users composing the images with lighting, perspective, constraints (telling it what not to do), and requests for people and how many. “Composition refers to requesting specifics about the structural arrangement of the scene, including placement of subjects, perspective, lighting, etc”

4. Interactions/Session Features “Interactions features look at the conversation as a whole and how people iterate on and edit generated images.”

5. Multi-Select Features These classify conversations across additional dimensions like prompts that include text and typography requirements, types of image transformation, work context, and stages of content creation. Multi-select Features provide additional information about what people are trying to accomplish and how they use image generation. The multi-select features includes: Full Specification Whether users precisely specify a style and wording.

Precise Content Only The user provides the text content but not the style.

Stylistic/Generic Only The user prompts contain the vibe of what they want but without specifics.

N/A The prompt doesn’t mention text or fonts.

The researchers found that Nano Banana was being used for more than trivial viral social media uses. People were also using it for commercial activities, educational illustrations, technical instructions, and product visualizations. The most surprising finding is that memes and humorous images were the least prevalent features in the social and viral categories. They found that the most prevalent feature was the inclusion of people (nearly 80%). Requests involving image composition and artistic styles were also common, while prompting the LLM to start over was about twice as prevalent as asking for minor changes. The researchers noted: “Perhaps surprisingly, meme style or format and absurdity / humor are the least prevalent.”

Lastly, the researchers discovered that much of the brand and marketing activity involved original, fictional, or unrecognized brands rather than established companies. The researchers suggested that some users may be developing branding for new or speculative businesses. They pointed to these findings related to the marketing usage of image generation:

Marketing Images Emphasized Precision Marketing usage emphasized specific visual requirements. The most prevalent features in marketing conversations involved controlling how images were composed, including the placement of elements, people, lighting, and instructions about what should not appear. Marketing Had The Highest Prevalence Of Detailed Text Requests Compared with the other four categories, marketing had the highest prevalence of requests specifying exact text and detailed typography instructions. This suggests that marketers are using image generation to create promotional images with specific text and design requirements rather than simply requesting attractive images. Small Businesses And Individuals More Prevalent Than Big Brands The Brand & Marketing category had the highest prevalence of conversations identified as involving small businesses, individuals, or side hustles. Marketing Uses Beyond Generating Images From Scratch The researchers identified activities involving refining logos, changing text and colors, creating promotional materials, and developing consistent visual brand identities, including assets for online engagement and traditional promotional uses. Takeaways

The researchers successfully used the Urania framework to conduct a “ privacy-preserving descriptive analysis ” to identify what users were doing with Nano Banana. They discovered that AI image generation is enabling a variety of business, marketing, and creative activities, including some that tasks that previously required professional experience that is now within reach of more people. They also acknowledged that it remains unclear whether AI is enabling entirely new activities or simply making existing ones less expensive. They expressed that they anticipate additional uses to emerge as people continue experimenting with AI image generation. articles.title: Google’s November 2026 Core Update Starts Rolling Out via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern
articles.fullContent:
Google began rolling out the November 2026 core update today, according to the Google Search Status Dashboard . The rollout started at 10:06 a.m. PT. Google says the update applies globally and to all languages and may take up to two weeks to complete.

The company’s Search Central account also announced the update on LinkedIn . It’s the third Search core update this year. Google recommends waiting until the rollout is complete before checking your Search Console data.

Google’s Search Status Dashboard entry reads:

“Released the November 2026 core update, which applies globally and to all languages. The rollout may take up to 2 weeks to complete.”

“This is a regular update designed to better surface relevant, satisfying content for searchers from all types of sites.”

The exact wording in that sentence is what Google used for its March core update .

As of posting time, no specific objectives are mentioned on either the dashboard entry or the LinkedIn post. The Search Central blog doesn’t have a post regarding the update either. Google’s core updates page carries a revision date of Dec. 10, 2025.

The May core update finished rolling out on June 2 , more than five months before today’s launch. Three spam updates ran in between.

September 2026 spam update : 13 days, 16 hours (Sept. 24 to Oct. 8)

August 2026 spam update : 2 days, 16 hours (Aug. 18 to Aug. 21)

June 2026 spam update : 2 days, 1 hour (June 24 to June 26)

May 2026 core update: 11 days, 21 hours (May 21 to June 2)

March 2026 core update: 12 days, 4 hours (March 27 to April 8)

The November update is the eighth ranking update listed on the Search Status Dashboard so far this year.

Some sites may experience rank changes during the rollout of the November core update. Google’s core updates document advises waiting at least a full week after the completion of a core update, then comparing your Search Console data from that week to a week prior to the start of the rollout. Google’s suggested baseline in advance of the November update is a week prior to Nov. 10.

A full two-week rollout would finish around Nov. 24. The week immediately following Nov. 24 will include U.S. Thanksgiving, Black Friday and Cyber Monday. Retail sites looking at this time period compared to a pre-update week would be looking at holiday traffic against a regular week.

According to Google, core updates don’t target specific sites or individual pages and are meant to keep its systems current as content on the web changes.

Per its LinkedIn post, Google will update its ranking release history page once the rollout is complete. We’ll update this article then, too.

articles.title: Google Releases Modern Web Guidance 1.0 For AI Coding Agents via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern
articles.fullContent:
Google issued version 1.0 of Modern Web Guidance, which is a free skill set that web development teams may use as an enhancement to their AI coding tools, in order for those tools to write code based on current browser features. The skills are in the form of packaged guidelines that the agent will look at while writing the code. The code generated by the agent will also be sent to the same pages that are evaluated for metrics such as Largest Contentful Paint (LCP), Interaction to Next Paint (INP), and accessibility.

Philip Walton, a senior staff developer relations engineer at Google, announced the release in a Chrome for Developers post. Version 1.0 adds an audit for existing code, and Firefox and Edge are joining the project. Chrome first released the guidance as an early preview at Google I/O in May.

Teams can install it by running npx modern-web-guidance@latest install in a project directory. It’s also available through the plugin marketplaces of most popular coding agents, according to the post.

Version 1.0’s audit will go through a project’s HTML, CSS, JavaScript files as well as its package.json to identify areas where developers are able to safely update their code, then walk the agent through the changes. This first iteration of the audit uses static analysis to look at a limited number of code patterns, according to the post.

The post says the library now targets “hundreds of verified AI knowledge gaps” across its guides. Additionally, current coding models continue to fall short in Google’s tests of accessibility, security headers, and loading priority for scripts and images.

According to Google, each of the guides is now reviewed and approved by a domain tech lead. For user-facing feature guides there is a dedicated accessibility review done by experts who use assistive technologies daily.

A governance document was uploaded to the project’s GitHub repository on Nov. 9 which outlines six owner seats for the project. Two of those seats belong to Chrome, Microsoft Edge and Mozilla each have one, and two are given to independent web platform experts. There is currently one open independent seat and no seat belongs to Apple.

Google’s announcement links to a public eval dashboard where coding agents from Anthropic, OpenAI and Google run the same set of tasks every night, with and without the guidance. A real browser then checks the DOM, styles and source code of each finished app.

When I checked Tuesday morning, guided runs were passing 88% of the automated checks, whereas unguided runs were passing 56%. These figures are based upon each agent’s combined results for nightly runs completed Nov. 8; the range is 199 to 215 tasks per agent. The dashboard provides a limited review (not a full WCAG audit, it says) of accessibility features such as support for keyboards, focus, and form labels.

Its task prompts don’t mention the guidance, so each agent has to work out on its own when a guide applies. In most of the recent suites listed, guided runs ran slower and burned more tokens.

Accessibility consultant Adrian Roselli evaluated the preview in May by giving Antigravity (Google’s AI coding tool) an animated accordion prompt found in the documentation. However, according to Roselli, the output did not comply with WCAG and its animation was not functional in Firefox. He also found no assurance that agents would be able to follow the guidelines. This was for the preview, not v1.0.

The new guidelines were tested by Japan’s creator platform, note inc. using two coding agents that ran through six user interface (UI) tasks across 180 test runs on clone versions of note inc.’s production code base. As explained in a Chrome blog , both agents’ scores on 19 browser checks rose after installing the skill without naming it in prompts, then again once prompts named it. Agent One went from 60.8% to 76.5% to 94.0%. Similarly, Agent Two had scores of 75.8%, 86.2%, and 90.0% under the same three test conditions.

One of note’s tasks checked whether the largest image in view on an article page had high priority and wasn’t lazy-loaded. The comparison table in the post shows that unguided agents wrote hero image code using both high priority and lazy loading.

The guidance is run by MetaMask, as part of an automatic review process for each pull request submitted to its open-source browser extension, according to a second Chrome post . Through Oct. 21 (the first five weeks), the bot identified 102 issues across 57 feature and fix pull requests. The engineers fully resolved 43 of them and partially resolved three of them. Another 16 were either declined or false positives. Twenty of them went unaddressed. The outcome of the other 20 is unknown.

Modern Web Guidance provides a no-cost means for teams to encourage agents writing code to use native browser capabilities and that includes code in existing legacy code bases. Most of the results that have been published are based on testing conducted by Google as well as customer testing that Google highlighted. Note Inc. tested the two agents using the same prompt with and without telling them to use the guidance; they both performed better when the prompt did tell them to use the guidance. The team can also label their prompts to include the guidance and keep field data and manual accessibility testing in the review.

Google says it plans to expand this process of auditing existing code at some point, as well as performing audits in which the agent is reasoning about the actual code being audited.

The company suggests pairing the guidance with Chrome DevTools for agents to allow the agent to run its own created code and test it inside of the browser. Preview users can use the command npx modern-web-guidance@latest update .

articles.title: Original content on social: Harder to find, but more important for brands to nail
articles.fullContent:
Throughout 2026, Sprout Social data shed light on a consumer contradiction: audiences began to reject AI-generated posts and want more original content, but they also feel it’s important for brands to keep up with culture and trends on social media.

A Q3 2026 Sprout Social Pulse Survey found that 33% of consumers think the originality of a brand’s content is what makes them stand out as a favorite on social media—second only to the quality of a brand’s product or service. But the same survey also found that 84% think it’s important for a brand’s social media to keep up with online culture.

Following trends and being original aren’t exactly complementary ideas. How can brands appeal to both of these expectations, and which matters more?

Original content offers an opportunity to break through crowded feeds and build long-term audience engagement. Luckily, there’s a way to produce original content while still paying homage to trends where you can offer a unique POV.

What (really) is original content?

At its core, original social content is an umbrella term for social posts that don’t just repeat viral memes, visual aesthetics or the same recycled take on a trend. While it might become a cultural touchpoint, original content can exist without the context of online culture. Audiences don’t need prior knowledge of internet lore to get it.

The best original content is highly entertaining, educational or both. And it comes from a perspective that only your brand can deliver. It connects people to your brand through human-driven storytelling that AI content tools can’t replicate. Put simply, it makes you feel something.

It’s also often episodic, weaving together a brand universe with a cohesive narrative and familiar faces. Like the Croc’s microdrama “Charmed to meet you.” It could even be inspired by a true story, like Actually Away, Away’s series inspired by a meet cute in Grand Central Station. Or, it could be heartwarming and earnest, like immi Ramen’s “Ramen on the Street” interview series.

Why original content on social matters more now

Brands are struggling to reach audiences and maintain engagement as social media saturation reaches its peak and AI fatigue sets in. Algorithms don’t serve up content like they used to, and a large follower count no longer guarantees that people will see your content. Discoverability requires a different formula that’s rooted in topical alignment to your audience’s interests.

Social teams aren’t creating content for the entire internet anymore. They need to reach niche communities within their audience segment, and doing so requires cultural understanding and scroll-stopping originality.

Originality rises above AI slop

Are all AI content creation tools bad? No. For example, AI tools can speed up manual hours of video and photo editing that significantly enhances the quality of content. Yet, they don’t have the human taste required to build something original—or compelling—from scratch.

Feeds have become inundated with AI-generated “thought leadership” posts, images and comments sections. At this point, the number of bots online have surpassed the number of human activity, and The Dead Internet theory is pushing audiences to tune out.

Sprout data from numerous surveys reinforced this idea. A Q1 2026 Pulse Survey found that 56% of consumers reported seeing AI slop on social media often or very often, with at least 83% seeing it at least sometimes. This influx of AI content is making audiences more selective about what they consume, with 50% of Gen Z and 44% of Millennials unfollowing, muting or blocking a brand or creator because they felt their content was AI slop.

What the data really tells us, though, is where the opportunity lives for brands. It’s the reason the word ‘lore’ was crowned the 2026 word of the year over ‘slop’ in Sprout’s 2026 Social Media Dictionary. People want depth, authenticity and uniqueness in their community spaces online.

There’s more room for brands to double-down on human-led, original content to actually capture fleeting attention, and refocus their AI investment elsewhere. For example, marketers say real-time audience insights would be the most impactful resource for their strategy. That’s where the real potential of AI lies—in analysis to garner timely insights.

Original content plays to audience and algorithm preferences

Resonant original content is striking. It holds your attention, inspires you, delights you, changes how you think. When you find it in your feed, you’re more likely to hit the share button, blasting the post across your DMs.

Shares are an important signal for marketers to determine how something was received. The 2026 version of word-of-mouth, shares are an endorsement that what you’ve created is worth talking about. Shares also serve the dual purpose of reshaping how users encounter content on social, especially on legacy networks.

As Lia Haberman articulated in this Instagram playbook, “DMs—not the Feed, not Stories, not Broadcast Channels—are the primary way people share on Instagram. We may never get back to a chronological feed but users have hacked the system to connect with their favorite people through DMs.”

Original content helps you tap into this discoverability engine by touching people’s hearts and minds, the attention economy’s true currency.

It upholds brand safety

The biggest moments on social also come with the biggest risks of copyright infringement. Brands that post about a pop icon marrying an NFL star, an athlete winning gold or the best big game ad are forced to use vague euphemisms or subtle references (see what we did there?)—unless they’re willing to face litigation. articles.title: Skydance to Embrace Bundling Across Business Functions
articles.fullContent:
$73 million – Paramount Skydance’s third-quarter net earnings before it acquired Warner Bros. Discovery in October.

$7 billion – Paramount Skydance’s revenue, a 5% year-over-year growth, before its acquisition was completed.

$6 billion – How much Skydance expects to achieve in run-rate synergies over the next three years.

20% – Rise in sports advertising commitments year-over-year for current and upcoming sports seasons leading into 2027.

Over the next few months and possibly years, bundling will take place at Skydance. After completing its acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery in October, the combined conglomerate is now looking to slim down and cut its roughly $80 billion debt.

In corporate speak, Skydance is looking to consolidate a lot of back-end and front-end operations. In regular parlance, this is just bundling, and the media company is looking to bundle much of what it has now to achieve these savings. It has started more than 20 of what it calls “workstreams” to identify areas of possible cuts.

The Skydance third-quarter earnings letter to shareholders said the company aims to reduce costs at least $2.2 billion by “bundling” redundant back-office and corporate functions. It aims to “bundle” its media planning and buying across business units to eliminate audience overlap, coordinate campaigns across those units and maximize media efficiency at scale.

Other areas will also see bundling, including technology. Skydance will unify its enterprise tech stack, streaming ecosystem and broadcast architecture, merging parallel technology functions. It will also bundle procurement and vendor management operations, saying its combined purchasing levels will provide economies of scale by consolidating purchasing decisions into one centralized group.

However, the one “bundle” consumers and subscribers will care about is direct-to-consumer products. Skydance announced in early 2027 it will bundle HBO Max and Paramount+. During the company’s third-quarter earnings call on Monday, CEO David Ellison said the two streaming services are complementary, and this was the “first step” toward offering a one-stop streaming service.

“This is a growth story; we are shifting from legacy media to building a next-generation media and entertainment company powered by creativity and technology,” said Ynon Kreiz, Skydance’s co-chief executive officer.

Mark Mwachiro is a TVNewser contributor who has been writing for the blog since March 2022. Based out of New York, Mark has also contributed to ADWEEK.

articles.title: Omnicom Makes Tom Schwenger CEO of Omnicom Health Marketing
articles.fullContent:
By Katie Duffy Omnicom appointed Tom Schwenger as chief executive officer of Omnicom Health’s marketing branch, the company announced last week.

Schwenger will manage Omnicom Health’s global marketing agencies. This role will entail developing and implementing client engagement models that cater to clients across the pharma, biotech, and consumer healthcare industries. The team, including Schwenger and the group’s agency leaders and integrated client leads, will continue to leverage Omni and Acxiom, Omnicom’s life science data and AI marketing intelligence platforms.

Schwenger will work alongside Michael Larson, chair of Omnicom Health, while transitioning into the role.

“I’m excited to join Omnicom Health at such a pivotal moment, leveraging the scale and capabilities of the newly combined organization to help clients navigate the rapid transformation across the pharma, biotech, and healthcare sectors,” said Schwenger. “This internal evolution, coupled with powerful market dynamics, creates an extraordinary opportunity to drive innovation and growth.”

Schwenger will be taking over the role from Dana Maiman, who served as Omnicom Health’s CEO for the past year. He brings more than three decades of experience driving growth and leading strategic initiatives in pharma, biotech, and healthcare. Schwenger was previously president and chief customer officer at Veeva Systems, a cloud computing company for the life sciences industry, where he encouraged early AI adoption and helped triple the organization’s revenue.

Omnicom Health’s appointment of Schwenger follows the organization’s acquisition of Interpublic Group (IPG), which formed the world’s largest advertising holding company. IPG Health, IPG’s group of healthcare marketing agencies, has been integrated into Omnicom Health’s network. Omnicom Health was recently named Healthcare Network of the Year at the 2026 MM+M Awards, further positioning itself as a leading force in the healthcare marketing industry.

articles.title: The 3 Paths to Being a Better Marketer That Have Nothing to Do with Marketing.
articles.fullContent:
By Jackie Cutrone Every CMO knows the drill: as a brand scales, founders and the executive committee reach out asking how to spot true marketing leadership in a sea of impressive resumes.

My answer is always the same: It’s not easy, but it is simple. Finding the right person requires looking beyond pedigree, predictable career steps, and whether they have done the exact job before. When I was hired by my CEO, he said 10 words I will never forget: “It’s not about what you’ve done, but who you are.” That sentiment still holds true today.

Only 6% of CXOs think the best profile for effective CMOs is a strong academic foundation. In other words, 94% of leaders who have a CMO reporting to them don’t think this is the best profile. But exclusive research conducted by NewtonX and ADWEEK for the Marketing Vanguard program reveals there is no single path to CMO effectiveness. Instead, it suggests the experiences gained outside of marketing are the secret to success.

Whether you’re formally educated or not, becoming a great top marketer is about the ability to gain and apply cross-functional experience. For example, it isn’t surprising that the top profile (24%) for a CMO leader is the “Hybrid Builder,” someone who combines academic marketing credentials with experience in product, sales, or consulting.  The second most popular profile (20%) is ‘no clear pattern,’ indicating effective CMOs can come from diverse backgrounds.

So what then are the diverse backgrounds that interest leadership? Commercial Operations, Entrepreneurship, and Data Science/Tech all rose to the top.

Those with Operations backgrounds represent 18% of responses. They have experience owning revenue, P&L, or general management. “It serves as evidence that they can connect marketing decisions to commercial performance and enterprise level outcomes,” says Jasmin Siegle, Senior Director of Strategic Insights & Analytics at NewtonX.

Entrepreneurs represent 16% and have experience operating under pressure. Having built or scaled a business signals comfort with ambiguity, resource constraints and accountability. All these are qualities that can help CMOs move beyond campaign execution and contribute more broadly to business strategy.

And in an increasingly measured and mar tech driven world, those with a data-science background are considered attractive cross-overs. Digitally native leaders also represented 16%. “Their value is not simply technical expertise; it is the ability to use data, technology, and analytics to guide decisions and demonstrate marketing’s contribution to measurable business outcomes,” says Jasmin Siegle, Senior Director of Strategic Insights & Analytics at NewtonX.

Taking a step back and looking at the similarities across disciplines, a picture emerges that suggests marketing effectiveness is defined more by behaviors and skills, not a single background or education.

For those that have it, appreciate your marketing education but don’t be complacent. The role is being rewritten in real time. There will always be something to learn. If your experience lies in a different field but you’ve always been interested in marketing, your skills are more transferable than you think.

Those who are best positioned for success are the ones who have the marketing background and education, and diverse cross-functional experience.

The research tells us that above all, everyone is on their own journey. Success rewards those who are proactive in benchmarking themselves and then creating steps-to-the-goal so they can possess the necessary skills for modern marketing leadership.

Jackie Cutrone is the Principal and Founder of Lightning Point Group. With nearly two decades in brand strategy and marketing, Jackie is the former CMO and current Chief Brand Advisor of NewtonX, where she architected the brand and demand engine from the ground up, driving 5x growth and effectively positioning NewtonX as the leader in AI-powered B2B research. Prior to NewtonX she led campaigns at Arnold, Havas and Interbrand, where she partnered with Fortune 500 brands such as American Express, Deloitte, AT&T, BNY, Gartner, Bain, LinkedIn, HP and dozens more. A recognized thought leader, she has authored industry-shaping content, led executive workshops, and spoken at Cannes Lions, WPP, IIEX North America, and ADWEEK events. Jackie holds degrees from Columbia University and the S.I. Newhouse School of Public Communications at Syracuse University. She has taught graduate classes at Columbia University and Pratt Institute.

articles.title: Meta Pauses Its Updated Business And Ad Terms Due Nov. 20 via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern
articles.fullContent:
Meta paused new ad and business terms scheduled to go into effect on Nov. 20. That leaves advertisers and other businesses using Meta’s services operating under existing terms. The pre-existing terms permit Meta to crawl content on advertiser websites for use such as “research and training,” whenever the advertiser places an ad order.

The Meta Business Help Center notice refers to the Commercial Terms, Product Catalog Terms, Self-Serve Ad Terms and Ad Creative Generative AI Terms. According to the notice, the updates “are now paused and will not take effect on November 20, 2026.”

On Nov. 5, Nieman Lab reported that Meta had posted the notice regarding halting the updates, and according to a Meta spokesperson, “We’re pausing the changes as we continue to engage with stakeholders and take our time to get this right.”

Meta says the four existing documents stay in effect until further notice. Each one’s page now opens with a line saying the updates are on hold. When I checked on Nov. 10, the U.S. and UK English previews of the updated Commercial Terms and Self-Serve Ad Terms showed a “page isn’t available” message.

The Commercial Terms currently in force, dated March 6, 2024, don’t include a crawling paragraph. The paused version would have added one covering sites associated with a business’s products or services. The Commercial Terms apply to any business use, including managing a Facebook Page.

The Self-Serve Ad Terms in force, dated Aug. 22, 2025, already include a crawling grant. By placing an ad order, an advertiser gives Meta the right to “access, index, cache, analyze or crawl” the content on its domains. The listed uses include developing advertising and other business-related products, “research and training,” and maintaining the integrity of Meta’s products.

The Ad Creative Generative AI Terms , dated May 6, 2024, also let Meta crawl URLs that advertisers provide, for use with their ads.

Adweek reported in October that the suspended Commercial Terms included a new section called AI Features. In this section, advertisers would be “solely responsible” for all of the results produced by Meta’s AI features as well as all changes those features make (including features that Meta enables automatically).

In its Ad Creative Generative AI Terms currently in effect, Meta has tied that responsibility to the advertiser’s own actions. The terms say that when an advertiser makes use of or posts AI-generated content, they are “solely responsible” for determining if the Output is correct, and if it is suitable for public display.

According to a Meta spokesperson who spoke to Adweek, advertisers can opt out of individual Advantage+ features at any time from within their Ads Manager account.

Businesses using Meta will not be required to consider any new business or ad terms prior to Nov. 20. For advertisers, the crawling allowance under the current ad terms will continue to apply when an advertiser places a new order; likewise, the terms granting this crawling allowance do not mention robots.txt.

The announcement from Meta says the company has made no changes to its crawling methods. Furthermore, the same options are available to content owners to express their crawl preferences via robots.txt.

Meta’s crawler documentation identifies Meta-ExternalAds for ads and various other business products. Additionally, the documentation identifies Meta-ExternalAgent for uses such as training foundation AI models. The documentation specifically includes robots.txt rules naming both of these crawlers, so review how you currently handle rules for both within your robots.txt file. The same page says two of Meta’s other crawlers might skip robots.txt in certain situations.

Meta says it’s still talking to the parties involved and that it’ll give an update once it has more to share. As of Nov. 10, the announcement hadn’t set a timeline for updating terms, nor had it specified whether or how much of the revised terms would be changed.

Nieman Lab reports that courts in Brazil and Norway have entered preliminary injunctions against these terms based on complaints made by press organizations. According to the UK’s Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) , its investigation is still open. It is investigating both the current terms of business for Meta and proposed changes to those terms. The timelines listed are subject to revision; currently the first phase of fact-gathering is scheduled to run through January 2027.

Key takeaways

  1. Share of voice measures how visible your brand is compared to competitors across social media, search, paid ads, and earned media.
  2. The core formula is simple: your brand mentions divided by total industry mentions, expressed as a percentage.
  3. Brands whose share of voice exceeds their market share tend to grow over time, which makes share of voice a leading indicator rather than a vanity metric.

What is share of voice?

Share of voice is a way of measuring your brand’s visibility compared to your competitors. It’s a great metric to focus on if you’re looking to increase brand awareness or sales.

This pie chart shows how share of voice splits among four competitors.

In the past, share of voice was used to measure the success of your paid advertising. Now the definition covers overall online visibility: social media mentions, news and blog coverage, where you show up in organic search, and how often your ads appear.

It’s also more than a visibility score. Research from Les Binet and Peter Field, published by the IPA in The Long and the Short of It, popularised the idea of “excess share of voice,” which holds that when a brand’s share of voice is higher than its share of market, the brand tends to gain market share over time.

The reverse is also true. That relationship is why marketing leaders treat share of voice as an early signal of where the business is heading, not just a snapshot of who is loudest.

In short: share of voice tells you what percentage of the total conversation in your category belongs to you.

What about social share of voice?

Social share of voice is a way to measure how much people are talking about your brand on social media. It’s usually measured as a percentage of total mentions within an industry or among a defined group of competitors.

In other words, traditional share of voice tracks what brands say about themselves, and social share of voice tracks what people say about brands. You can also think of it as when social listening meets competitive analysis.

For example, if your brand sells running shoes, you should expect to show up in conversations about running, running shoes, and sneakers. Share of voice will give you an idea of how often your brand comes up compared to other brands in the same space.

Understanding your social share of voice puts all of your other social media analytics into context.

What is the difference between share of voice and share of market?

Share of voice and share of market sound similar but measure different things.

  • Share of voice tracks attention: how much of the conversation, coverage, or ad space in your category belongs to you.
  • Share of market tracks money: what percentage of category sales or revenue you actually hold.

The useful part is the gap between them. Share of voice moves first, share of market follows. If your share of voice is well above your share of market, you’re building the kind of awareness that usually converts into sales later. If it’s below, competitors are buying attention you’ll likely have to win back at a higher cost.

Track both together. Share of voice tells you whether your marketing is working; share of market tells you whether it paid off.

  • Budget and resource allocation: Put money where your visibility gap is widest
  • Campaign effectiveness: Benchmark before and after a launch to see if it landed
  • Customer engagement and sentiment: Understand not only how often you’re mentioned, but how people feel about you

Online reputation management software monitors, tracks, and helps you respond to brand mentions, reviews, and sentiment across social media, review sites, news outlets, forums, and search results. While social media monitoring focuses on what’s happening on platforms like Instagram, TikTok, and X, online reputation management also covers review sites, search engine results, news coverage, and online forums.

  • Review sites: Google, Trustpilot, Yelp, and industry-specific platforms
  • News and media: Articles, press coverage, and blogs
  • Forums and communities: Reddit, Quora, and niche message boards

What are social video metrics and why do they matter?

Social video metrics are the numbers that show how your video content performs on social media platforms. They track how often your videos are watched, how people interact with them, and what actions viewers take after watching.

At their best, video marketing metrics don’t just tell you what happened, they show you why. These are the insights that help shape smarter content, better social media campaigns, and a stronger connection with your target audience.

Some examples of social video metrics include:

  • View count: How many times your video was played.
  • Watch time: How long people stayed engaged.
  • Engagement rate: How often viewers interacted (likes, comments, shares).
  • Video completion rate: How many viewers watched all the way through.
  • Play rate: What share of people who saw your video actually pressed play.
  • Click-through rate (CTR): How often viewers clicked on your call-to-action (CTA).
  • Shares and saves: Indicators of content that resonates and drives social sharing.

These metrics matter because they’re how you measure the actual impact of your video strategy. They help you understand what’s working (and what’s not), refine your creative and messaging, and compare performance across social channels.

Key takeaways

  1. Social-first AI is AI designed specifically for social media, using real-time social data rather than static web content to power insights, content, and trend detection.
  2. Most general-purpose AI tools are adding work, not saving it, with 43% of social media managers spending 11+ hours a week on AI tools.

What is social-first AI?

Social-first AI is artificial intelligence designed around social media data and social media workflows. Instead of drawing on general web crawls with a training cutoff, it works from live signals across social platforms, so the insights and content it produces reflect what people are talking about now.

The distinction matters because social moves differently from almost every other marketing channel. A trend can form and fade inside 48 hours. Tone shifts by platform, by audience, and sometimes by week. General-purpose AI for social media tends to flatten all of that into something safe, generic, and slightly out of date.

Most social-first AI systems share a few defining characteristics:

  • Real-time data foundation: Insights come from live social conversations, not static training data with a knowledge cutoff.
  • Platform-native understanding: It recognizes that a LinkedIn post, a TikTok hook, and an Instagram caption are different jobs with different norms.
  • Proactive trend detection: It surfaces emerging topics while there’s still time to act, rather than summarizing what already happened.
  • Social-specific tone and context: Outputs reflect how people actually talk online, including the references and formats native to each channel.
  • Governed outputs: Answers are traceable to sources, and content moves through approval workflows before it goes live.

Put simply, social-first AI treats social as the primary data source and the primary workflow, not an afterthought bolted onto a general marketing tool.

How does social-first AI compare to general-purpose AI?

The core difference comes down to grounding. General-purpose social media AI tools are strong at language and weak at timing. Social-first AI is built so that timing, tone, and platform context are part of the answer, not something your team has to add afterward.

Why does general-purpose AI fail social teams?

General-purpose AI fails social teams because it wasn’t designed for the pace or style of modern social. The problem isn’t that AI lacks potential, or that its underlying algorithms are flawed.

These tools promise automation but require micromanagement. This is unsurprising when only 16% of marketing work is currently AI-automated. They surface information but lack context, and they’re trained on data that rarely reflects what people care about right now.

If we zoom out more, a clear disconnect emerges between how leaders think AI is performing and how it’s actually landing on the front lines. 64% of senior marketers believe their tools use real-time data, but only 39% of social media managers agree.

Marketing leaders are far more confident in their AI’s real-time data than the practitioners using it daily.

As AI budgets rise and expectations grow, the cracks are starting to show. The people closest to the work, closest to the platforms, the conversations, and the trends, know the truth: most AI-powered tools can’t keep up.

And when your tools can’t keep up, neither can your team. Instead of solving problems, most AI-driven tools are actually creating more work for already busy social teams. Here are three reasons AI is falling short, and what needs to change for social strategies to actually benefit.

Is AI actually saving social teams time?

For most teams, no. AI is adding hours rather than saving them. It was pitched as the time-saver social teams have been waiting for, but in practice, it’s become a big time sink.

43% of social media managers now spend more than 11 hours a week using AI tools. That’s a full third of their time spent coaxing content out of tools that were supposed to eliminate busywork.

What is content moderation?

Content moderation is the process of reviewing, filtering, and responding to comments, messages, and other user-generated content on your social channels.

The goal is simple: make sure real people get real responses, while spam, trolls, and harmful content get filtered out.

The practice has changed a lot. What used to be a queue of comments reviewed by hand is now a mix of AI-assisted filtering at the first pass and human review for anything sensitive or ambiguous. One thing to keep in mind: moderation isn’t about deleting every negative comment to make your brand look perfect, and it’s not about censorship either. The goal is to remove harmful content, not silence constructive criticism.

articles.title: How to add alt text to social media images fast
articles.fullContent:
Social media alt text is easy to skip and expensive to skip as well. Skip it, and you lose the readers who browse with a screen reader. You weaken your content’s chances of surfacing in search. And you fall short of a social media accessibility standard your customers now expect brands to meet.

You don’t have to choose between doing it right and doing it fast. This guide will explain what alt text is, why it matters and how to write it well. We’ll also show you the one-click way to write alt text for social media images at scale.

Sprout Social’s Essentials plan lets you quickly add alt text to your social media images. Open the image in Compose, click Add Alt Text, write a description and save. Or Sprout’s AI Assist analyzes your image and drafts alt text in one click for you to review, edit and publish.

What is alt text on social media?

Alt text, short for alternative text, on social media is a written description attached to an image so screen readers can describe it to people who can’t see or load it.

It fills in what a visual would communicate on its own. People with low vision or those browsing with images turned off still understand your complete post.

Alt text is not a post caption. It’s not a place for commentary, image credits, keywords or calls-to-action. Those add noise for people using screen readers. If the text doesn’t describe what’s in the image, it doesn’t belong in the alt text field.

Facebook, Instagram, LinkedIn, X, Threads and Pinterest all support native alt text fields. Type alt text on each app as you post, or add it across multiple networks in one pass using a publishing platform like Sprout Social.

Why does alt text matter for social media marketers?

Alt text puts your message in front of more people, including those who can’t see the visuals. Adding alt text also makes accessibility a regular part of your publishing routine, which builds credibility and strengthens your brand image.

Does alt text improve accessibility?

Yes. Accessibility is the primary purpose of alt text.

The World Health Organization estimates that 1.3 billion people live with a significant disability. Many use screen readers to turn content into speech or braille. Alt text gives them the information, humor, emotion and context your visual carries.

Alt text also supports people on slow connections or who turn images off to save data. When an image doesn’t load, its description still tells what you shared.

Can alt text help with social media SEO?

Alt text supports social media SEO when it includes words that accurately describe the image and matter to your audience. When it’s written to please an algorithm, it fails the accessibility test and rarely boosts your ranking.

For example, “Three ceramic planters on a white shelf” includes “ceramic planters,” a term your audience may already search. It also gives social platforms more context to surface your content than:

  • “Our latest collection” (too generic)
  • “Best ceramic planters pots sale free shipping” (irrelevant keyword stuffing)

Describe the image accurately, and include the terms that belong there anyway. Discoverability follows.

Is alt text required by policy?

Alt text may be required by your organization’s accessibility policy or applicable laws, depending on your industry, location and audience. Check which requirements apply to your brand.

Even when it’s not mandatory, people expect accessible content from brands. Major social networks also offer tools and accessibility guidance to help.

Adding alt text alone doesn’t guarantee legal compliance. Add it to your publishing checklist alongside captions, transcripts, strong color contrast and clear link text.

What are alt text best practices for social media images?

Good alt text gives people enough detail to understand the image without a long description. Here’s how to keep yours useful:

  • Keep it short but descriptive. Aim for 125 characters as a common guideline. Go longer when the image needs extra explanation.
  • Skip “image of” or “picture of.” Screen readers already announce that an image is present. Start with the description and save your readers the redundancy.
  • Weave in keywords naturally. Include relevant terms only when they describe what’s in the image. Skip search phrases that add nothing to the description.
  • Add context around your visual. When it makes sense, explain why the image is paired with the post. For example, “A line graph showing customer response time falling from six hours to two” is more useful than “A blue line graph.”
  • Leave out hidden messages, credits and calls to action. These distract from the description. Put them in your caption, where everyone can access them.

How long can alt text be on each network?

HTML doesn’t set a character limit for alt text, but social networks and publishing tools do. For example, X allows up to 1,000 characters while Pinterest allows 500. LinkedIn’s publishing API allows up to 4,086 characters but recommends staying under 120.

If you’re publishing through Sprout Social, the following limits apply:

Network Character limit X, Facebook, Instagram, LinkedIn Up to 1,000 Pinterest Up to 500

You don’t need to use all that space. We suggest around 125 characters as a general guideline. Go longer when readers need more detail to understand the image.

How do you add alt text to social media images manually?

Add alt text to your social media images from the same Sprout Compose window you use to draft the rest of your content.

First, log in to your Sprout Social account. New to Sprout? Sign up here and connect your social profiles. Then follow the steps below:

  1. Go to Compose and select the profile(s) you’re publishing to.
  2. Attach an image to your post.
  3. Click the pencil icon on the image.
  4. Click Add Alt Text.
  5. Write your description within the network’s character limit.
  6. Click Save.

An alt text indicator will appear on the image in both Compose and your Publishing Calendar.

Manually adding alt text works. But writing every description from scratch, one image and one post at a time, is where the hours begin to add up.

Why is manual alt text a time drain for growing brands?

Manual alt text takes time because every social media image needs an accurate and relevant description. As your publishing calendar grows, so does the work of writing, checking and adding those descriptions.

If you post images daily across four or five networks, you have dozens of alt text fields to fill each week. Carousels multiply the work, since each image needs its own description.

The work is worth doing. The hours are not. Every minute you spend typing descriptions is time you can’t spend on strategic campaign planning and community management.

Key Takeaways

  • An XML sitemap should include the canonical URLs you want search engines to crawl and index, not every URL on your site.
  • Dynamic sitemaps are the best choice for most websites because they update automatically as pages are added, removed, redirected, or changed.
  • Keep <lastmod> dates accurate and reserve them for meaningful page updates so search engines learn to trust the signal.
  • Google ignores the <changefreq> and <priority> tags, so there’s no SEO benefit to including them.
  • Google Search Console can turn your sitemap into a diagnostic tool by showing which submitted URLs are being discovered and indexed.

Most websites have an XML sitemap. A lot of those sitemaps aren’t optimized, though. 

That means site owners are missing a golden opportunity to improve their SEO and gain an edge over competing brands.

Your sitemap gives search engines a roadmap to the content you want them to find. When that roadmap is full of redirects, non-canonical URLs, or outdated content, search engines have a tougher time doing their jobs.

This forces them to spend time sorting through URLs you don’t really want them to index.

A well-optimized sitemap, on the other hand, gives search engines a more direct path to your most important content. It helps new and updated pages get discovered sooner and keeps search engines focused on the pages you most want them to crawl and index.

In this guide, we’ll look at what belongs in your sitemap and what doesn’t. I’ll also show you how to structure your sitemap to help search engines crawl your site more efficiently.

What Is an XML Sitemap?

In simple terms, an XML sitemap is a file that lists the URLs you want search engines to know about. Think of it as a table of contents that helps crawlers understand what content is available on your site.

    (“XML” stands for “Extensible Markup Language,” a way of structuring and sharing information.)

    A sitemap gives crawlers a direct path to important URLs, so they don’t have to rely entirely on links to discover them. This is especially useful when important pages sit deep within your site or aren’t well connected through your internal linking.

    AI and LLM crawlers can also reference your sitemaps when discovering URLs, turning an optimized sitemap into yet another way to help your content get discovered by AI platforms alongside Google and Bing.

    A basic sitemap entry only needs to provide a few useful pieces of information:

    • Where the page is located: <loc>https://www.example.com/mypage</loc>
    • When it was last significantly updated: <lastmod>2026-09-30</lastmod>

    You may have seen <changefreq> and <priority> in older sitemap examples. Google ignores both, so there’s no reason to include them these days.

    Having a sitemap is only the starting point. If it’s filled with outdated or redirected URLs, you’re not getting nearly as much value from it as you could. So, let’s look at how to optimize it.

    Dynamic vs. Static Sitemaps: Which Should You Use?

    Two types of sitemaps exist today: static and dynamic.

      A static sitemap captures the URLs on your website at a particular point in time. The problem with this is that your site doesn’t stand still. 

      Publish a new page, remove an old one, change a URL, or redirect a page, and your static sitemap becomes outdated. That is, unless you regenerate it each time you make a change.

      However, a dynamic sitemap can keep up with these changes. It automatically updates as your site evolves, so search engines always get the most accurate view of the URLs currently live on your site. For most websites, this is the better choice.

      You don’t need to be an SEO expert to build a dynamic sitemap yourself. Many content management systems and website platforms can generate them for you.

      WordPress users can use plugins like Yoast SEO or Rank Math, while platforms like Shopify and Squarespace have built-in sitemap functionality.

Sprout Social’s very first Social Intelligence Summit brought together industry leaders for a series of discussions focused on that idea, from spotting early signals to turning them into real business action.

Summit takeaways from across the sessions

  • Build permission before the moment you need it: Speed is blocked by approvals, so agree on guardrails, decision owners and a checklist in advance.
  • Relevance beats reactivity: Not every trend is right for every brand. Ask whether it fits, adds value and is something you can move on quickly before jumping in.
  • Social intelligence should change business decisions: The best stories turned conversation into action, like all-day breakfast and the Ziploc cereal bag or Dubai chocolate.
  • Translate for each stakeholder: Insights stall unless you frame them in the language and priorities of leadership, legal, product and other teams.
  • People are both the signal and the megaphone: Fans, ambassadors, employees and community managers are where signals start and where you can amplify your message.
  • Start small: For small teams, look to change things where you have influence.Take one signal to one team to achieve one outcome.
  • AI assists while humans decide: Use AI for summaries and efficiency, but keep a human in the loop and avoid content audiences recognize as AI-generated.

Here’s a deeper dive into the key takeaways from each session.

Keynote: How real-time social signals shape timing in marketing

Jay Schwedelson, founder of SubjectLine.com and CEO of Guru Media Hub, kicked off the summit with his keynote address on real-time social signals in marketing. His message was a blunt one; that marketing teams should stop guessing and start knowing. His agency runs around 40,000 campaigns every year, and he argued that your customers and your competitors’ customers are already telling you what you should do next. All social media marketers have to do is listen to them, then turn those insights into action faster than anyone else.

Social intelligence isn’t about collecting more data. It’s about actually making better decisions before anyone else does. Jay Schwedelson
CEO, Guru Media Hub

His first example focused on competitor complaints. Schwedelson suggested pulling the last 90 days of comments on three competitors’ posts and sorting them into buckets. Potential buckets included but weren’t limited to pricing, product failures and missing features. The next step is to pick a complaint your product solves or does better, and put out an us versus them post. The beauty of this is you don’t even have to name the competitor, if you’ve done your research correctly it’s something that people are already feeling, so they’ll naturally associate the negatives with the competitor. Though the origin of this is social, the profile of the people engaging are almost certainly already customers or considering buying, so this is mid-funnel or even lower-funnel work. Posting the same comparison on your website can also help with AI search, giving it a wider impact.

Timing was the second theme. When a platform launches a feature, it often gives a boost to the people who adopt it early. That means moving first can buy visibility. The same logic applies to culture. When a trend gets going, if you join a viral moment in the first 48 hours, your brand looks relevant; wait much longer than that and your brand looks behind. Citing Sprout’s 2026 Social Intelligence Report, Jay noted that only 10% of brands are able to act on an insight from social within hours, while 86% of organizations report missed opportunities because of delayed or siloed insights. His fix is a trend-to-campaign playbook with set guardrails and named decision owners. This ensures you don’t miss the moment while you’re still doing the rounds collecting approvals internally.

The critical thing in social media is moving at the speed of culture Jay Schwedelson
CEO, Guru Media Hub

He closed with two practical rules:

  1. Put paid budget behind posts that already work organically rather than trying to force success.
  2. Avoid generic AI-sounding language like “unlock”,”elevate” and “optimize”. Use the language your customers actually use instead.

Our first panel focused on the question social teams all over the world face every day; how do you tell a real cultural shift from a fleeting viral moment?

Panelist: Josh Rangel, Senior Director of Social Strategy, Ogilvy
Panelist: Tulani André, VP of Social Content and Creator, Zolando

André encouraged audiences to focus less on the timing. Plenty of short-lived trends are still worth joining, so what matters is whether the moment and the trend itself fit with your brand, its goals and its voice. If it’s 24 hours later and there still isn’t an obvious on-ramp for you to join the conversation, then it probably isn’t for you.

Rangel added that frameworks are your friend here. He recommended a checklist and an action plan that asks whether a trend is relevant, whether you can move quickly and whether you have something worth saying. Passing on one trend won’t cost the brand because there will always be another one. He also noted that approvals often stall with brand managers, legal and leadership. To avoid this, he advised educating those groups ahead of time, agreeing with legal on where the line is and showing leadership how trend work benefits the company in language they understand like sentiment and awareness.

Returning to the idea of frameworks, readiness is what makes speed possible. André’s team sent social managers to Scotland on two days’ notice to film on the set of Troye Sivan’s new video. They could do this because they already had repeatable content franchises and a team they trusted.

TikTok lets you use AI, but requires creators to add a label when it’s used to create or significantly edit realistic-looking people or scenes.

What Is Answer Engine Optimization?

AEO is here to stay. Make sure you have an AEO strategy to capitalize on it.

articles.title: How to Teach Content Strategy to Stakeholders Who Don’t Speak Marketing
articles.fullContent:
Key Takeaways

  • Content strategy buy-in often breaks down in translation to non-marketers, even when the strategy is sound.  
  • Lead with what your stakeholder already measures. How a strategy ties back to organizational cost, risk, or speed means more to them than marketing buzzwords. 
  • Call attention to problems or poor performance yourself. Clarify any wrong conclusions and present solutions before stakeholders have time to spiral. 
  • Name what stays the same before you name what changes, so new tactics feel familiar to your audience. 
  • General recommendations rarely get implemented. Give your audience specific action items in a portable checklist or one-pager. 

Most content strategies don’t fail on their merits. They stall out because content strategy buy-in never arrives from the person who funds the work, approves it, or executes part of it. That might be a client-side VP, your own executive team, a sales director, or a legal reviewer who has never opened your editorial calendar. 

The data supports the gap. Content Marketing Institute research ranks cross-department collaboration among the top content marketing challenges for 21 percent of B2B marketers. 

Content marketers get very good at doing the work but still struggle to convince stakeholders how necessary it is. Those are separate skills, and we need plenty of practice in both. 

If you feel like you’re failing to get the right stakeholders on side for your strategy, read on. You’ll learn how to explain content strategy to non-marketers, so they understand the rationale enough to defend it (even when you aren’t in the room). 

Teaching Is a Different Skill Than Doing

When stakeholders deny or ignore content strategy, we usually blame the audience. Leadership doesn’t get it. The client won’t listen. Sales ignored the brief (again). 

That explanation feels comfortable, but it’s not always the truth. The question is, how well are we explaining ourselves? 

The same pattern shows up in every department. A client executive, a product manager, and a compliance reviewer all evaluate your recommendation against a different set of priorities. A decision that looks obvious to a content strategist can read as a cost or a liability to someone who only thinks about content for 20 minutes a month. 

Stakeholder education in content marketing is a learnable skill, not a personality trait. Nobody is born knowing how to translate a content audit into CFO speak. You practice, watch what explanations tend to land, and adjust. Here’s what I’ve found works consistently. 

Start with the Stakes, Not the Solution

Lead with why the decision matters to the specific person in front of you, in their terms, before you name a framework or tactic. This does more for getting buy-in for content strategy than any deck you build. 

Attention follows relevance. Open with a scenario that matches your stakeholder’s priorities, then connect your recommendation to it. 

Use this same move across different audiences: 

  • A budget holder hears a content refresh as spend on something already done. Reframe it as efficiency. You’re reinvesting in assets that already earn traffic instead of funding net-new pages that take months to mature.  
  • Legal hears a byline requirement on articles as more review work eating up their time. Reframe it as attribution control. Named authors with verifiable credentials reduce the risk of unsourced claims attributed to the company. 
  • Sales hears a webpage restructure as a cosmetic change. Reframe it as speed. Clear subheads and direct answers let a rep send one link mid-deal instead of writing a custom explanation. 

Translate your content strategy into the currency your audience already trades in, then explain the specifics where you need sign-off. Most collaborators tune in if you’re covering cost, risk, or speed. 

Beyond buzzwords, root your argument in data they recognize. A content strategist lives in organic sessions, keyword rankings, and time on page. A sales leader watches pipeline contribution and deal velocity; a CFO watches customer acquisition cost and ROI. You don’t have to drop your own metrics, just connect them. Bring the organic sessions that became pipeline; tie your rankings to the deals they influenced. Pull evidence from the dashboard they already open, then draw the line from your metric to theirs. 

Defuse the Scariest Interpretation Before They Invent It

Nearly every content strategy shift arrives attached to an alarming headline. A traffic decline. A ranking drop. A platform change nobody controls. 

The Pew Research Center tracked 68,879 Google searches and found click-through fell from 15% to 8% when an AI Overview appeared. Read that insight cold in a quarterly review and your client hears one message: our investment is evaporating. 

Speak to those concerns before they raise them. State the numbers plainly, then correct potential wrong conclusions immediately. Something like this works: “organic clicks are getting harder to win on informational queries as search engine trends shift, which is why we’re moving effort toward pages that convert and toward becoming the source these systems cite.” 

Skipping an uncomfortable number doesn’t make it disappear. Your audience fills in the blank themselves, usually with something worse than reality, and you find out during Q&A after you’ve lost the floor.

articles.title: How to use social media audience segmentation to drive smarter business decisions
articles.fullContent:
For brands, social media is a goldmine of real-time insight into consumers’ preferences, behaviors and motivations. And segmenting social users intentionally—using live conversation data rather than static demographic details—empowers leaders to make smarter business decisions, whether it’s optimizing spend, discovering new markets or driving revenue.

But social media audience segmentation isn’t a one‑off marketing exercise. It’s a dynamic, cyclical process designed to spot emerging opportunities and inform data-grounded strategies.

With the help of this guide, you can better understand how to approach social media audience segmentation and use it to make an impact across the business.

What is social media audience segmentation?

Social media audience segmentation is the process of breaking down your target audience that’s engaging on social networks into smaller, distinct groups based on shared characteristics, behaviors or interests.

In contrast to broader marketing segmentation, social segmentation draws on real-time social data. Think live conversation, engagement and sentiment data, rather than CRM or survey inputs that may reflect the past and not a user’s present feelings.

Segmentation is one of the many pillars of social media intelligence, helping organizations move beyond broad audience assumptions by uncovering the distinct groups driving conversations online. Teams can then make more targeted decisions aligned to the current pulse of the market across customer care, product innovation, campaign planning and overall business strategy.

Why audience segmentation matters more than ever

One of the key factors driving the need for segmentation is the degradation of trust and attention among consumers.

According to the Q1 2026 Sprout Pulse Survey, consumers are becoming more particular about what they engage with online, with two-thirds (66%) feeling more selective than a year ago. AI slop (i.e. undifferentiated, one-size-fits-all content) was cited as a contributor to eroding trust; 56% of respondents said they see AI slop often or very often.

Many brands are mistakenly investing in this generic content. This ultimately results in wasted budget as platforms are increasingly rewarding relevance over reach.

Segmentation is what enables brands to achieve personalization and, in turn, resonance with their audiences—without necessarily needing to increase headcount or budget.

4 types of social media audience segments (and where social data fits)

Let’s take a look at four key types of social media audience segments, what they tell you and the social signals that paint the picture of who they are.

Demographic segmentation

Basic demographics like age, gender or follower count are a reasonable starting point in creating social media segments. This data is garnered via self-disclosure (i.e. a user inputs this information when creating a profile), network-level audience demographics reported by ad managers or analytics tools.

While these details don’t tell you much on their own, they can reveal behavioral trends. For instance, you may see a generational skew depending on the networks and content formats a person engages with. In general, Instagram Reels and TikToks attract a younger audience, while Facebook’s most active users skew older.

However, it’s important to note that demographics don’t provide the soundest basis for segmentation because the data is often self-reported. Users may skip fields or deliberately enter false details to protect their privacy or access age-restricted content.

Demographic-based targeting is also losing its predictive power. Per the 2026 Influencer Marketing Report, only 17% of consumers check follower count before following a creator. For nearly half of respondents (47%), things like content topic and behavior matter far more.

With that in mind, demographics should be used as a starting point rather than a primary segmentation driver. Instead of examining people’s surface-level traits, look at the things they say and do unprompted on social. These signals are more dynamic and indicative of how people identify themselves.

Psychographic segmentation

Psychographics is the classification of people based on psychological criteria—such as values, attitudes or motivations—that influence their engagement and consumption patterns.

To segment your social audience by psychographics, review their comments, posts and shares. The content they post or engage with can tell you a lot about their internal beliefs. Your brand can then use these insights to tailor its content and target these users more closely.

For example, if your audience members regularly post about climate change and sustainability, you can place them into an environmentally motivated segment. From there, you can center your messaging around subjects related to your brand, like ethically sourced materials, reusable products or community initiatives.

Behavioral segmentation on social

While psychographics focus on what users believe, behavioral segmentation shines a light on how they behave on social. The actions they take, the conversations they partake in and the content formats they engage with.

To build behavioral segments, brands must observe audiences’ patterns. How often do they post? What formats do they share (e.g. static images, carousels, Reels)? What are they talking about in comment sections? Whose posts are they commenting on?

Finding the answers to these questions can unearth important information about consumers’ decision-making and motivations. In addition to seeing how people behave, you’ll begin to understand why. You won’t just see who they interact with, but who they really are behind the screen.

Say you identify a segment of users consistently participating in giveaways, promo codes and engaging with shopping-on-a-budget content. With this data, you can glean what might be most important to them when making purchase decisions: fair pricing and discount offers. From there, you can tailor your social messaging accordingly, whether it’s highlighting affordable prices or sharing the outsized value of your offerings.

Geographic segmentation

A person’s physical location shapes their social and spending habits—and the two often go hand in hand.

Various social signals enable brands to glean a user’s whereabouts, including location tags, geotagged posts and stories, and the language or dialect they use on social. Additionally, some network behaviors and preferences are region-specific.

Key Takeaways

  • The 4 Ps (product, price, place, and promotion) are tools marketers use in combination to shape how a product (or range of products) is positioned, promoted, and sold to a specific group of customers. Together, they’re often referred to as the “marketing mix.”
  • The marketing mix is fundamentally a tech-agnostic framework for helping with important marketing decisions. 
  • “Product” looks at how well features meet needs, “price” at what customers are willing and able to pay, “place” at the best ways to distribute a product, and “promotion” at building market awareness. 
  • Well-known companies like Rolex, McDonald’s, and Red Bull have perfected the 4 Ps behind their products and brand identities.
  • AI is changing how marketers execute the 4 Ps, but the fundamental questions behind product, price, place, and promotion remain the same.

The 4 Ps of marketing (product, price, place, and promotion) have been around for decades, and they still drive decisions around every successful product launch.

Also known as the “marketing mix,” they help you think through how to bring a product to market and reach the customers most likely to buy it.

It doesn’t matter if you’re running a one-person small business or a global enterprise. The 4 Ps help you bring a product to market and get it in front of people most likely to buy it.

How you put the 4 Ps to work has changed, though. AI is giving marketers new ways to understand their customers and make more informed decisions, often in less time.

I’ll cover some of these opportunities as I show you how the 4 Ps still drive marketing decision-making today.

What Are the Four Elements of the Marketing Mix?

The 4 Ps of marketing, commonly known as the marketing mix, stand for product, place, price, and promotion. They’re like four levers companies can adjust to better position their products for the customers they want to reach.

Here’s the meaning behind each of the four Ps: 

  • Product: What you’re selling, including its features, packaging, and the support that comes with it
  • Price: What you charge and how you structure the pricing
  • Place: Where and how your customers can buy the product
  • Promotion: How you get the word out about the product

To more fully understand the 4 Ps of advertising, we need to take a step back. Mention “marketing,” and most people think of customer-facing content like ads, social media posts, emails, videos, and blog articles like this one. 

In fact, these represent just one piece of a much broader discipline. They’re the “promotion” part of the mix called marketing communications.

True marketing is a big-picture process that strives to meet all customer needs. And thinking in terms of the 4 Ps allows companies to do exactly that. 

What About the 7 Ps and the 4 Cs?

The idea of a marketing mix has been around longer than the 4 Ps themselves.

In 1948, Harvard professor James Culliton described marketing executives as “mixer(s) of ingredients.” Inspired by this idea, fellow Harvard professor Neil Borden often referred to the concept of the marketing mix in the years that followed. 

Then in 1960, marketing professor E. Jerome McCarthy organized it into the four elements we know today in his book Basic Marketing: A Managerial Approach.

Other models have been suggested in the years since, with two in particular gaining traction: the 7 Ps and the 4 Cs:

  • The 7 Ps: In 1981, marketing professors Bernard Booms and Mary Jo Bitner expanded the 4 Ps to better suit service-based businesses. Their model adds people, process, and physical evidence to the mix. These cover the employees who deliver a service, the delivery process, and the environment where business takes place. 
  • The 4 Cs: Marketing professor Robert Lauterborn proposed a more customer-oriented alternative to the 4 Ps in 1990. His model replaces them with consumer wants and needs, cost, convenience, and communication. Instead of starting with what a business wants to sell, the 4 Cs push marketers to focus on what customers actually need. 

These alternative models add some useful nuance. To me, though, the 4 Ps still make up the strongest foundation for marketing campaigns. articles.fullContent:
It’s certainly not 2010 anymore. So why are so many businesses still resourcing social media teams as if it is?

Social teams have evolved far beyond publishing posts and responding to comments. Today, they manage content and video production, influencer partnerships, customer care, social search, paid media, community engagement and increasingly, social intelligence.
